THE BIG PICTURE: MSU hockey looks to jump-start season with rivalry test against No. 1 Michigan The Spartans got off to a slow start, allowing a goal in the first six minutes while the Wolverines registered the first 11 shots on target. U-M would make it 2-0 on a goal from freshman forward J.P. Hurlbert (a 2026 Detroit Red Wings draft pick) with just over eight minutes remaining in the first period to bring the crowd back alive. The Spartans would get one back in the dying moments of the first period, with freshman Jack Hextall winning an offensive zone face-off back to freshman defenseman Tommy Bleyl, who then fed the puck down low back to Hextall, who delivered a pass through the U-M crease. Forward Cullen Potter, who shifted to the wing for the first time this season Friday, was there to jam the puck past goaltender Jack Ivankovic with just 21 seconds left in the first period to give the Spartans some momentum. MSU carried that into the second period, outshooting U-M 16-6 with multiple solid chances, but Ivankovic stood firm. U-M would later get a 3-on-1 rush the other way, and defenseman Asher Barnett beat MSU goaltender Joshua Ravensbergen to restore U-M's two-goal lead. The Wolverines would score twice more early in the third period, and then the fireworks began. MSU sophomore defenseman Sean Barnhill laid a big hit on U-M forward Nick Moldenhauer at the Michigan blue line, sparking a big scrum with Barnhill getting a two-minute minor for boarding and each side receiving matching roughing calls. With things seemingly settled down, MSU senior defenseman Patrick Geary went over to the U-M bench, sparking a number of Wolverine players to react and prompted all three MSU players to leave the penalty box and start the brawl again. Additional discipline could be handed out by the Big Ten after reviewing the incident. Ravensbergen made 33 saves for the Spartans, who fall to 6-4-1 on the season. sports.title: Jaguars score early, shut out nationally ranked Sals for soccer title
sports.description: FREDERICA – Appoquinimink scored just four minutes into the DIAA Division I Boys Soccer Tournament final. In a sport where goals are rare and very difficult to get, it was a sweet and satisfying start. It also meant perennial powerhouse Salesianum, ranked 15 th in the nation, had the added incentive to score and 86 minutes in which to do it. The Sals could not, and Appoquinimink won a state championship that will long be as cherished and coveted as such accomplishments can be Nov. 20 at DE Turf. Freshman Caiden Stone scored that fourth-minute goal and the Jaguars spent the rest of the game thwarting one Salesianum opportunity after another, including two in the final minute alone. “It was just everybody,” senior captain and center back Gabriel Arbuet said. “Everybody worked their tails off. Last game of the season. Seniors especially, last game of their careers. “We just worked hard the whole entire time. We knew what was on the line. We knew we could make history. It was a whole team effort.” Third-seeded Appoquinimink (16-1) was playing in its sixth state boys soccer championship game, all since 2013, every one against Salesianum. The Jaguars prevailed in only one of those, the 2020 final on a tie-breaking penalty-kick shootout, which was their last title-game appearance. “We had a game plan going into it,” Appo coach Lance Berry said. “We worked on it the past two days and the boys executed perfectly. “So hats off to Sallies. They're a hell of a program. They're the standard. But our boys showed up tonight. Really proud of each and every guy.” Top-seeded Salesianum (15-3), its national ranking courtesy of the United Soccer Coaches, had beaten Appo 2-1 on Oct. 22. But both teams had conceded afterward that, with Appo missing three starters that night, a rematch might be even more competitive. It most certainly was, especially with the determination Salesianum gained with that early deficit. But the Sals, who’d won 20 of the last 24 state soccer titles and were appearing in their 17 th straight title game, couldn’t level the match despite numerous opportunities. Sometimes, perhaps out of a sense of desperation, they may have unleashed shots too early and from too far away rather than working for something better. Berry was happy to point out that the Jaguars set a school record with their 13 th shutout, having won all three state tournament games 1-0. They allowed five goals all year. “The defense has been lights out all year,” said Berry. “To be honest with you, I'm not too surprised . . . When we had all of our guys healthy, they have given up maybe a goal when they're all on the field.” Berry has now won boys and girls state titles as coach at both his alma mater Caravel and Appo. He again joined his dad John, who steered McKean to the 1984 title and was in attendance, on the list of championship coaches. sports.title: Raines denied in Jacksonville's first-ever Open Division football game
sports.description: JACKSONVILLE | He trudged through Duval County mud and across the goal lines adjacent to Moncrief Road to history four times, and Brian Wilson Jr. couldn't remember the last night that felt anything like that. "Maybe Little League?" the Miami Columbus running back guessed. The first-ever Florida High School Athletic Association Open Division game ever played within Jacksonville city limits was a winner for Wilson. But not for the home crowd, or the hometown champions. Watch Florida high school playoffs live on NFHS Network Got a great play? How to submit your high school sports highlights to the Times-Union Fueled on offense by Wilson's four touchdowns, and stifling the reigning state champions from start to finish, Miami Columbus closed the door on Raines' Open Division hopes and downed the Vikings 28-6 on Nov. 20 at the Graveyard. For the first time in six years, the 2025 state champion Vikings (10-2) have lost consecutive games, after going down 28-7 at West Boca Raton on Nov. 13 in the round-robin Open Division format. A gritty effort from a depleted Raines defense wasn't enough against the Explorers (11-1), who frustrated the Vikings throughout a night of wind-driven tropical downpours. But to end in the win column, Columbus needed the four scores from Wilson, the sophomore power back splitting carries with Northern Illinois-bound senior Cecil Smith. "After four touchdowns," Wilson said, "I feel amazing right now." MISCUES DERAIL RAINES' HOPES After sophomore Sa'Mon Ellison-Morgan took a 15-yard quarterback keeper up the middle with 4:30 remaining in the first quarter, tying the score 6-6, Raines seemed ready to match the state's second-ranked squad highlight for highlight. It didn't turn out that way. The Columbus defensive front seven, highlighted by Chanavis Chance Jr., Tyler Tindal and Damien Harvey, plugged the rushing lanes and harassed Ellison-Morgan (2 for 13, 6 yards) all night. Harvey, the 265-pound nose tackle, recovered a fumble and picked off a pass off a Tindal tip. Meanwhile, five-star Miami commit A'mir Sears patrolled the secondary and made two tackles for loss on attempted Raines misdirection plays as the Explorers limited the Vikings to six first downs and 37 total yards. Raines also struggled with three bad exchanges on punts, all of them setting up the Explorers with prime field position. At one stage, Columbus began six consecutive drives in Viking territory, ranging from the 9 to the 41. VIKINGS' DEFENSE BATTLES ON With Super 11 edge rusher Troy Butler and linebacker Johdeem Jones both out, and defensive end Chenaniah Doran playing only limited snaps in his return from injury, Raines' defense battled to stay in the contest for a while. Wary of the messy conditions, Columbus played a ball-control game, with Smith (29 carries, 133 yards) and Wilson (13 carries, 77 yards) grinding out yardage. But for much of the night, Raines kept them out of the end zone, including key fourth-down stops from Nate Bennett and Tysen Marsh

sports.title: Berlin football holds off Middletown, clinches its 5th straight playoff berth
sports.description: Berlin's Gamaliel Ayizano, 4, tries to push his way past Middletown's Juel Ocasio, 54, during the CIAC football game between Middletown and Berlin high schools.Friday, November 20, 2026, Sage Park, Berlin, Conn. (H John Voorhees III/Hearst Connecticut Media) BERLIN - The Berlin Redcoats are in. If there's any justice in the football world, the Middletown Blue Dragons will also qualify for the postseason, because on Friday night at Sage Park both teams showed they belong there. In a Central Connecticut Conference game played six nights before Thanksgiving, but befitting the playoff stage that will follow the holiday, Berlin clipped Middletown 35-32 to beat its neighbor to the south and qualify for the CIAC tournament for a fifth straight year. This baby was by far the closest of the five. What appeared to be a TKO when Berlin scored on the third play of the game and then recovered a fumble on Middletown's first snap instead turned into a 15-rounder that wasn't over until Berlin junior wide receiver Anthony Frayler secured an onside kick with 37 seconds left. Both teams scored five touchdowns. Both teams finished 7-3. The difference lay in Berlin junior Noah Foster going 5-for-5 on extra points and Berlin's defense stopping Middletown on all but one 2-point conversion try. A 31-yard touchdown run by Foster, coming with 1:56 left out of Berlin's new-wrinkle Wildcat, proved to be the game-winning score. Middletown, which had hung tough behind touchdown jaunts of 75, 15 and 60 yards by junior running back Nick Cyril, answered that Foster score to keep hope alive. Junior QB Matteo Fletcher, coming on early in the second half when starter Brendin Smith went down with an injury, hit senior Sebastiano Bibisi with a 38-yard pass on a fourth-and-10, then rifled a 12-yard TD pass over the middle to senior Victor Bonet. Berlin stuffed the 2-point run, then recovered the ensuing onside. And with that, last year's Class M state champ clinched a berth in the Class SS playoffs. Middletown remains in the top eight in Class MM at 7-3 and will secure a berth if any of the 6-3 teams on its heels - Fairfield Prep, Platt and Torrington - lose their regular-season finale next week. Even if all three win, Middletown might still get in on bonus points. On Friday night, the Redcoats drew opening blood on a 43-yard TD run by junior Brandon Sadowski on toss-right out of the double-wing. Also for Berlin, senior running back Gamaliel Ayizano broke off a 62-yard scoring dash straight up the middle, Frayler corralled a 30-yard TD pass down the right sideline from junior QB Chace Hrubiec and junior RB Nick Balicki muscled in a crucial score late in the first half on fourth down from the 1 after Middletown had made three stops inside the 3. The Blue Dragons got on the board via a 60-yard pick-six from Bibisi. Foster and Sadowski had interceptions for Berlin. Junior Liam DeSantos had the fumble recovery on Middletown's first snap. Cousins was designated for assignment on November 17 as the Dodgers added four pitching prospects to the 40-man roster , and was in roster limbo before getting cut loose by Friday’s MLB deadline to tender contracts to all players. It’s been more than two years since Cousins pitched in the majors. He was limited to two rehab games in 2025 before undergoing Tommy John surgery that June . He signed a one-year, $950,000 contract with the Dodgers on the day before opening day in 2026 , and pitched in six more rehab games in September for Triple-A Oklahoma City. For the Comets last season, Cousins allowed five runs in his six games, with five walks and four strikeouts in 4 1/3 innings. Now 32, Cousins had four year, 91 days of major league service time and would have been eligible for salary arbitration this winter. Both MLB Trade Rumors and Cot’s Baseball Contracts predicted the right-hander to earn $1 million in 2027 . Cousins also has an option year remaining, having used options in 2022 and 2024. But that wasn’t enough to keep him on the 40-man roster.

sports.title: Darian DeVries wants the Indiana-Kentucky rivalry series to continue
sports.description: Nov 20, 2026; Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; Indiana Hoosiers head coach Darian DeVries looks for an intentional foul against the Kentucky Wildcats during the second half at Lucas Oil Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect A lot has changed from when Indiana and Kentucky agreed to resume their longstanding annual rivalry series in men’s basketball. Darian DeVries took over as head coach for the Hoosiers ahead of the first matchup in the 2025-26 season, which was Mark Pope’s second year as the head coach of the Wildcats. Neither was in their position when the series was agreed upon, with Mike Woodson and John Calipari leading their respective programs at the time. Resuming the series was a priority for Woodson, who took a game at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis rather than Assembly Hall in Bloomington to get it done. Now it’s DeVries’ program and he, like Woodson before him, wants the Wildcats on future schedules. DeVries, coming off of a 90-76 win over Kentucky in that very game in Indianapolis on Friday night, was asked if he’d like the series to continue in the future, beyond its current four-game slate. “I would love to keep it going,” DeVries said. “I think it’s great for college basketball and it’s fun games for everybody. The fanbases, proximity, to have two historic programs like this continue to play non-conference… yeah. We would love to continue to do it.” Indiana will return to Lexington next year before getting its one game at Assembly Hall in 2028. Join the conversation! sports.title: Illinois breaks program, Big Ten record for three-pointers in game
sports.description: CHAMPAIGN, Ill. — Illinois started the season with a bang, making the most three-pointers in a game in program history in the 120-45 win over FDU. That record held up for just four games before the Illini broke it again. Friday against EIU, Illinois drained 23 threes to beat the previous record of 19 in the 114-52 victory. The Illini nearly surpassed the record in the first half, making 15 shots from beyond the arc. Midway through the second half, Stefan Vaaks put up a three-pointer from the corner and drained it, giving the Illini 20 to break the program record. Just seconds later, Ethan Brown hit his seventh three from beyond the arc to bring the team’s total to 21. A few minutes and misses later, a Zavier Zens triple found the bottom of the net, breaking the Big Ten record for the most three-pointers made in a game. The previous Big Ten record was 21, which Purdue tied earlier Friday evening. 22 3-pointers! Brown led the way, sinking a career-high seven of this 11 three-point attempts. sports.description: EAST LANSING – Depleted at quarterback. Banged-up at running back. Out of bodies at linebacker. All of the injuries finally caught up to Michigan State football . And there was nothing the Spartans could do – no matter how hard they competed and fought through them – to stop No. 14 Oregon. The Ducks started slow, thanks in part to another staunch defensive showing early by MSU before losing Brady Pretzlaff early in the first half and fellow linebacker Dion Crawford early in the third quarter. Oregon used a trick-play touchdown at the end of the first half and pounded the Spartans in the second for a 45-7 victory Friday, Nov. 20, at Spartan Stadium. INSDIE THE SPARTANS: MSU and Oregon QB shuffle proof CFB is business 1st, education 2nd Starting quarterback Alessio Milivojevic did not play and backup Cam Fancher also was out for MSU (3-8, 1-7 Big Ten), and it is unclear of their status heading into the finale next Saturday at Rutgers. Kayd Coffman started his second game this season, and the true freshman finished 10-for-19 for 106 yards and an interception. He was sacked once before being taken out early in the fourth quarter for redshirt freshman Leo Hannan with MSU trailing, 38-7. The Spartans also were without linebacker Jordan Hall, starting safety Devin Vaught, starting nickelback Michael Richard and starting defensive tackle Ben Roberts. On offense, along with its top two quarterbacks, MSU was missing starting left guard Conner Moore, its top two tight ends (Brennan Parachek and Jayden Savoury), starting wide receiver Rodney Bullard Jr., and running back Cam Edwards, among others. Quarterback Dylan Raiola went 21-for-34 for 234 yards with a touchdown for Oregon (8-3, 6-2), but 103 of his yards (including his 31-yard TD pass to Dakorien Moore) came in the fourth quarter after the Ducks entered the final period with a 24-point lead.. It was over when ... MSU’s offense found limited traction with Coffman at quarterback and with running backs Brandon Tullis and Jaziun Patterson clearly not at 100% health-wise. However, the Spartans trailed just 10-0 while holding a 115-86 edge in yardage going into Oregon’s final drive of the first half. After a penalty to start the Ducks’ possession, MSU defensive tackle Eli Coenen sacked quarterback Dylan Raiola for 5-yard loss. Oregon was facing second-and-20 at the Spartans’ 5 with 1:36 to go, and Pat Fitzgerald called timeout. The Ducks’ Brandon Smith ripped off a 19-yard run out of it and then barely converted on third-and-1. Raiola rediscovered his rhythm, with completions of 16, 18, 13, 3, 3 and 7 yards to get into MSU’s red zone and field goal territory. His deep shot sailed out of the end zone with 7 seconds left, and kicker Gage Hurych trotted onto the field for a 33-yard field goal attempt. Fitzgerald again called timeout to get his field goal block unit on the field. And Oregon again stunned the Spartans. technology.title: Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
technology.description: Amazon is of two minds when it comes to automated purchasing. The ecommerce giant has been busy banning AI shopping agents from accessing its website. Meanwhile, AWS Marketplace has opened its door to bot-based buying. "Buying software and data through AWS Marketplace just got easier, for you and for the AI agents working alongside you," said Mya Papolu, product marketing manager for AWS Marketplace and Partner Services at Amazon Web Services, in a blog post this week. "For re:Invent 2026, we’re launching capabilities designed to reduce friction across the buying journey." For a company that has blocked bots from Google, Meta, and OpenAI, and sued Perplexity to keep its AI-encumbered Comet browser away, the openness of AWS Marketplace to agentic commerce invites questions. We asked Amazon to explain but we've not heard back. AWS Marketplace is allowing AI agents to scour its site and buy some cloud software products using the x402 agentic payment protocol , which is supported by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments. Introduced by Coinbase and Cloudflare , x402 got handed over to the Linux Foundation earlier this year, and now has support from a variety of tech platforms, including AWS, Google, Stripe, and various blockchain networks. About a week ago, Brave Software announced support for x402 payments through its search API. AWS requires sellers to register with AWS Marketplace and to integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK to enable agentic product purchases. Transactions settle in USD through AWS billing so existing spending controls can be applied. And now, customers in the US can buy some AWS Marketplace software without an AWS account; instead they're asked to provide an email or social media login, and a credit card. While AWS Marketplace today lists mainly familiar software categories (Business Applications, Data & Analytics, DevOps, Infrastructure Software, and so on), AWS has a broader product inventory in mind. Beyond software and APIs, the biz sees a future in selling content and data. Papolu announced that AWS is now selling " data as a service ." "Data providers can list their offerings in AWS Marketplace, making commercial data accessible to both human teams and the agents working alongside them via the AWS Marketplace website, APIs, and MCP server," she said. This includes services like Moody's Credit MCP server for financial research; Reuters Geopolitical News for AI-structured reporting; US Building Permits, Contractors & Residents Data from Shovels; and US-EN Multi-Speaker Conversational Acoustic Corpus from Uber AI Solutions. In canned remarks provided to AWS, Nandhan Puppala, general manager at Uber AI Solutions, said that data quality and readiness can help advance AI products. technology.title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
technology.description: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation , responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP ( 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline . Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. technology.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
technology.description: The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state's right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations. AT&T's status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027. The order released today granted AT&T's request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC's previous approval of AT&T's petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California's rules in July. Read full article Comments

technology.description: Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search. Read full article Comments

technology.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
technology.description: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. technology.title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
technology.description: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register . “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. technology.description: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." technology.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
technology.description: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven , and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions. Read more Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago. “This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. Advertisement The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers . These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention. He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. science.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
science.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment. Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics , the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon. In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies. "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement . "That shouldn't be the Wild West." Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons. The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games. With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19). Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November. Communication issues for Perseverance Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth. It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress). In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers). Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer. Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems. The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday . Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna. This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras. The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7 . But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA. "The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue." science.description: null For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades. This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography. What's happening and when to look Aldebaran, the brightest star in the constellation of Taurus. (Image credit: Christophe Lehenaff via Getty Images) Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky. The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula . Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun . If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way , the familiar arrangement would fall apart. science.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
science.description: null The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time. Did an eclipse rewrite the Pyramid Age? Pharaoh Shepseskaf's huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara (Image credit: Jon Bodsworth - www.egyptarchive.co.uk) We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse. Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing. Is the oldest recorded eclipse hidden in the Bible? Researchers have proposed that an annular eclipse occurred over Canaan on Oct. 30, 1207 BC, and may be described in the Bible. science.description: null Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . Information within the report, which you can read here , is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought. Up-front finding The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits." Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites , which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security." While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests. There are a range of threats to space-based services, both commercial and military. Some are reversible, while others are not. (Image credit: DIA) Counterspace worries A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen. Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system. Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report: Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries. Physical or cyberattacks against ground sites and other terrestrial infrastructure supporting space operations can also threaten satellite services. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse. This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest. Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4Q November 17, 2026 Why is it incredible? From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission , even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range. It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home. Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. science.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. science.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
science.description: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. science.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule heads home to Earth from the ISS
science.description: null SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has begun its journey home to Earth. The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) today at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China. If all goes according to plan, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at about 4:55 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). There will be no livestream for its reentry and splashdown. (Today's departure webcast did not feature live footage of the moment of undocking, as it occurred during a gap in coverage of the high-bandwidth signal needed for video.) The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it's the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15 , delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It will bring a lot of stuff down to Earth, too. "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17). "The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth ," they added. Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.
